header:
Date: 2025-10-15
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Rossi (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (NimbusFin Lead ML Eng), Tom Reyes (NimbusFin Infra), Sanjay Patel (NimbusFin CTO)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest benchmark results comparing Redwood's hosted setup vs the customer's baseline provider. Redwood showed improved p95 latency by ~12% on the 8k prompt workload after KV cache and batch tuning; baseline had higher throughput on single-stream large-batch tests but spun up different instance types. Action items agreed: share raw logs, run extra tuning with explicit batch sizes and quantization profile, customer to share baseline config and compliance needs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Aisha: Aisha here. Tom and Sanjay are on.
[00:12] Luca: Luca from Redwood, hi.
[00:15] Tom: Tom, infra.
[00:18] Sanjay: Sanjay, CTO.
[00:21] Maya: Great. Agenda — benchmark recap, tuning notes, next steps. We sent the spreadsheet earlier this morning. Any issues accessing?
[00:31] Aisha: I have it open, yeah. Quick note, some of the column headers looked slightly different from the baseline CSV, so I just want to call that out.
[00:40] Luca: Totally, we changed p95 vs p99 naming, sorry for that. The raw traces are attached in the folder.
[00:46] Tom: OK cool.
[00:50] [01:05] Luca: On slide 2, the short version — for the 8k token prompt distribution, with KV cache enabled and batching at 8 we saw average latency drop and p95 improve by ~12% compared to your baseline run. The baseline provider used a different instance type, I think c-series 32g, so not apples-to-apples.
[01:28] Aisha: We did the baseline with their recommended config, yes, c32x-ish. Also they had quantization turned off for fairness.
[01:36] Luca: Right. We ran two configs: quantized 4-bit and float16. Quantized gave similar throughput but a bit wider variance on p99 in long streams.
[01:48] Sanjay: Can you say numbers? p50/p95/p99?
[01:52] Luca: Sure. For the 8k workload — Redwood hosted quantized: p50 120ms/token, p95 220ms/token, p99 320ms/token. Baseline: p50 140ms, p95 250ms, p99 420ms. Throughput (tokens/sec) was comparable but baseline had higher peak throughput in a single long-batch test because they used bigger batching on their node.
[02:23] Tom: When you say 'bigger batching' that's like batch size 64/128?
[02:26] Luca: Correct, they tested large-batch throughput at batch 128 which boosts tokens/sec but increases tail latency; for our real-time SLOs we keep batch sizes lower and rely on continuous batching and KV cache to keep cost low.
[02:40] Aisha: Important — our app needs 99th percentile under 500ms for interactive flows; the p99 numbers you shared for quantized look ok but baseline p99 was at 420ms which is borderline given our other network hops.
[02:55] Maya: Good call. One nuance — our hosted runs used our multi-tenant pool in us-east-1; you mentioned baseline ran in us-west — do you want us to re-run in us-west to match region?
[03:07] Tom: That would help rule out cross-region latency.
[03:10] Sanjay: Also we need to consider dedicated capacity for predictable p95, there's cost tradeoff.
[03:16] Maya: We'll include dedicated estimates in the pricing doc. Luca, did you see any memory pressure or OOM in your runs?
[03:23] Luca: No OOMs. For the float16 runs memory was fine; quantized runs had smaller memory footprint but we saw occasional variance at p99 due to kernel scheduling — we've filed an internal tweak to the kernel selection which should smooth that.
[03:37] [04:00] Aisha: About caching — can you describe how KV cache helps for our prompt patterns? Our prompts have fairly long context but a lot of reuse of knowledge snippets.
[04:12] Luca: Sure. KV cache lets us reuse prefix activations so repeated system/context windows don't get recomputed; in our numbers cache reduced token compute for repeated turns by roughly 30–40% depending on reuse ratio. That lowers both latency and cost. There's a tradeoff with memory and eviction policy but for your session-based flows it's a big win.
[04:36] Tom: Any security implications for KV cache? We need to know retention and how it's encrypted.
[04:41] Maya: We'll attach the security whitepaper, but short answer — KV cache is ephemeral per session, stored in memory on-host, encrypted at rest for dedicated deployments and never persisted to customer S3 unless customers opt-in.
[04:55] Sanjay: SOC2 and KMS integration — does Redwood support customer-managed keys?
[04:58] Maya: Yes for Private and Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; hosted can optionally use customer-managed keys via our KMS pass-through in enterprise packages. We'll share the SOC2 docs in the follow-up.
[05:12] [06:00] Luca: Back to tuning — we recommended three knob changes: batch_size 8/16, enable prefix KV cache, and quantization profile q4_0 for parity. When we did that, p95 moved from ~250ms to ~220ms. The cost dropped by ~18% measured as token compute units.
[06:28] Aisha: On cost — that 18% is compute only, right? Not including network or extra infra?
[06:33] Luca: Correct, it's compute unit reduction; we'll break out networking and infra in a separate column.
[06:38] Tom: How reproducible were the runs? We saw some run-to-run noise in the baseline tests.
[06:42] Luca: We ran 10 seeds per config — variance in the long tail due to scheduling and kernel choices. We're including standard deviation in the next spreadsheet version.
[06:52] [08:00] Aisha: One concern from procurement — baseline provider offered a price break if we commit to reserved instances; how do Redwood reserved capacity prices compare?
[08:10] Maya: Dedicated/reserved capacity gives predictable throughput and a per-month commit. Our Commercial team provided a starter number in the PRD; I can put a dedicated scenario next to the committed baseline cost so you can compare apples-to-apples.
[08:24] Sanjay: We will need an explicit SLA for latency if we go dedicated.
[08:28] Maya: Yes, dedicated comes with SLA options and an escalation path. We'll include SLA text in the follow-up.
[08:33] [09:00] Tom: Regarding the baseline provider config — I'll upload their exact docker runtime flags and instance types to the shared drive. That should help you match.
[09:09] Aisha: If you could also rerun Redwood in the same instance family we can better compare.
[09:14] Luca: We can provision a dedicated node with matching instance type for a parity run. We'll note the infra delta in the spreadsheet.
[09:21] [10:00] Aisha: A couple of technical notes — our workload often has bursts up to 2k RPS for short periods; how does Redwood autoscaling behave?
[10:30] Luca: Autoscaling is policy-driven; for hosted we have burst capacity and pre-warming heuristics. For Dedicated you can have reserved pools and burst over-provisioning if needed. For your 2k RPS bursts we'd recommend a hybrid approach — reserved baseline plus autoscale for spikes.
[10:47] Sanjay: For compliance we might prefer dedicated so we can get KMS and audit logs in our VPC.
[10:54] Maya: That's a common path. We'll provide the Private/Dedicated checklist.
[11:00] [15:00] Luca: Quick note on model variants — we tested a Redwood-verified model variant tuned for latency; baseline used stock upstream weights. That explained some of the delta. If you want strict parity we can run upstream weights but we generally recommend our tuned variant for production.
[15:23] Aisha: Ok we want both: parity run plus tuned run, so we can compare quality + latency.
[15:30] Luca: Makes sense. We'll schedule both.
[15:40] [20:00] Tom: One weird thing we saw — baseline had better throughput on long batch tests but had significant p99 spikes when the node rotated. Any idea why?
[20:12] Luca: Could be their scheduler or kernel mismatch. We saw similar spikes early in their runs when they used mixed instance families.
[20:20] Aisha: Also, how do you handle degraded fallbacks? If one region is overloaded, will Redwood fall back to a different model or region?
[20:30] Maya: Yes, smart routing policies can fallback to compatible model variants or another region depending on your SLA and data residency settings. We can configure silent fallback or explicit error escalation.
[20:42] Sanjay: Need to confirm data residency — some EU customers need all processing inside region.
[20:48] Maya: We support region pinning for requests and private control plane for on-prem. We'll include cookie-cutter language in the security pack.
[21:00] [25:00] Luca: For the follow-up runs we'll produce: (1) parity run on matched instance types, (2) tuned run with q4_0 + KV cache + batch 8/16, (3) dedicated node run to show SLA tail behavior. Each will have p50/p95/p99 and throughput and raw logs.
[25:23] Aisha: Good. On quality — do you see any regression in generation when using q4_0 vs float16?
[25:30] Luca: Minimal on our internal evals; we'll run your prompt set to check for regressions and include a BLEU/ROUGE-ish and human spot-check sample.
[25:40] [30:00] Tom: About the raw logs — what's the format? We need to ingest them into our perf dashboard.
[30:10] Luca: CSV for latency buckets plus optional JSON traces with timestamps. We'll standardize the field names to match your baseline CSV layout.
[30:20] Aisha: Please keep the names consistent — last time we had to manually remap.
[30:25] Luca: Noted.
[30:30] [35:00] Maya: Recap and next steps — we'll send the updated benchmark spreadsheet and config, Luca will run three follow-ups, Tom to upload baseline config, and we'll reconvene after results. Any other blockers?
[35:18] Sanjay: Procurement will want a legal redline for the pilot terms — is that possible?
[35:24] Maya: Yes procurement can review a pilot MSA. We'll loop legal in next thread.
[35:30] Aisha: One last ask — can you include a quick cost model per 1M tokens under both reserved and on-demand?
[35:36] Maya: We'll include a per-1M-token cost estimate for hosted on-demand and a monthly committed dedicated number.
[35:42] [40:00] Tom: Alright, thanks everyone.
[40:03] Luca: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[40:06] Maya: Thanks all. We'll target sending results and docs by next Friday.
[40:12] Sanjay: Thanks.
[40:15] Aisha: Thanks, bye.
[40:18] [END]
